source.title: Information Capacity: Evaluating the Efficiency of Large Language Models via Text Compression
source.authors: Cheng Yuan; Jia-Wei Shao; Chi Zhang; Xue-Long Li

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests cross-scale NLL prediction with its information-capacity method and compares it with a single-reference power-law prediction. This is a different method from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit or test power-law curves for held-out cross-entropy against parameter count, tokens, or compute, nor does it find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. It evaluates NLL prediction using information capacity and compares that with a cited Kaplan power-law formula. The pretraining-token comparisons in Table 3 report NLL changes but do not test whether those changes follow a power law. The downstream benchmark correlations use information capacity rather than scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: Section 4.4 applies the Kaplan single-reference power law (alpha_N = 0.076 from the original paper) to Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 72B. It reports errors of up to about 26% and argues the power law is a less robust predictor across scales. This is a result bearing on V2, though in a weak form: the exponent is borrowed rather than fitted on small runs of the same setup. The paper's own information-capacity predictor and its MMLU correlations do not measure any version and belong in fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that information capacity is nearly constant within a model series, and that tokenizer efficiency, pretraining data and MoE are its main drivers. They argue it enables accurate single-reference cross-scale NLL prediction, more robust than the Kaplan power law with its published exponent, and that it correlates with benchmark scores in matching domains.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes an information-capacity calculation based on compression gain and inference FLOPs; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure. It separately applies the cited Kaplan single-reference power-law formula as a comparator.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction errors vary with the prediction method and reference/target model sizes. The paper also reports that information capacity and model rankings depend on evaluation dataset, but those results do not test the scaling-law claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Single-reference NLL prediction from constant within-series information capacity is accurate in the tested Qwen series: ±3% for Qwen3, -6.02% to 7.73% for Qwen2.5, 0.50% for Qwen1.5 0.5B to 72B. This implies compression gain is linear in log inference FLOPs, rather than a power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a model series, (text size per token minus NLL plus an offset) scales proportionally with log inference FLOPs, allowing cross-scale NLL prediction from one reference model.

fits_no_version.finding: Information capacity correlates with MMLU, most strongly when measured on an English corpus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compression-efficiency metrics predict downstream scores in the matching domain.

record.problems: The prediction evidence is limited to the model series and datasets reported; errors are mostly presented in figures, and no uncertainty estimates are given. The study does not test fitted training-loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible version-linked results were left out. The individual cells of the prediction-error heatmaps are not separately entered; the text-stated aggregate ranges and the explicitly stated Qwen1.5 example are recorded instead.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Tables 3 and 4 show NLL falling with size and with pretraining tokens, but no functional form is fitted.
No power law is fitted on small runs of the study's own setup and extrapolated. Only Kaplan's published exponent is transplanted onto Qwen2.5.
No controlled comparison of depth, width or other shape choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.
Benchmark scores are related to information capacity, not to scale or pretraining loss.
No exponent fitting or comparison of fitting choices. The failure of the borrowed exponent hints at setup dependence, but the cause is not isolated.

missing.what: NLL against pretraining tokens: TinyLlama-1.1B at 0.5–3T tokens; Qwen2 at 7T vs Qwen2.5 at 18T. Decreases are irregular, with diminishing returns attributed to data quality. Descriptive only; no power-law fit, so it cannot determine V1.
Full Figure 7(b) error range for the Kaplan power law (-20.94% to +26.48%), with the sign pattern by direction of extrapolation.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law comparison is a strawman-like test for V2. It uses Kaplan's exponent unchanged, with no irreducible-loss term, on different data, tokenizer and training regimes, and indexes size by inference FLOPs. It therefore qualifies the transferability of published exponents (relevant to V7) more than it tests extrapolation from small-run fits. A reader could instead treat it as a weak T3 or as not testing V2 at all. The study is a preprint, and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute; no test over several orders of magnitude under non-bottleneck conditions.
Tests a cited single-reference Kaplan power-law prediction on Qwen2.5 NLL estimates, not power-law fits across other models, training-loss curves, or general settings.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimising parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No tests of the claimed power-law form in other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study correlates benchmark scores with information capacity, not with scale or pretraining loss.
No investigation of how power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations change with setup or fitting choices, or of curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 series
rows.operation_detail: Estimate FineWeb-Edu NLL across model sizes from one reference model using the Kaplan et al. (2020) power-law formula.

conditions.value: Single reference model; reference sizes vary across the sweep
Kaplan et al. (2020) power law, αN = 0.076

rows.value: Estimation error may exceed 25%; predicting a larger model from a smaller reference generally overestimates NLL, while the reverse prediction heavily underestimates it.
rows.note: The authors describe the power-law estimates as significantly biased. This row concerns the power-law comparator, not the paper's information-capacity predictor.
rows.check: The value is vague. Figure 7(b) gives errors from -20.94% (0.5B estimated from the 72B reference) to +26.48% (72B estimated from the 0.5B reference). Errors grow with the size gap, and adjacent sizes are mostly within a few percent. The exponent is taken from Kaplan (WebText2, Kaplan's tokenizer and parameter counting) and not fitted on small Qwen2.5 runs. The formula has no irreducible-loss term, and the models are compared by inference FLOPs/size, not training compute. The row should record these conditions.

relationships.condition: Kaplan published exponent (alpha_N = 0.076) applied by single-reference extrapolation to public Qwen2.5 base models 0.5B–72B, FineWeb-Edu NLL
relationships.reason: r1: errors grow with the size gap, reaching +26.48% (0.5B to 72B) and -20.94% (72B to 0.5B). A published exponent transferred to a different data, tokenizer and training setup does not extrapolate accurately. Because the exponent was not fitted on small runs here, this qualifies V2 rather than refuting it.
relationships.display_finding: Single-reference errors reached +26.48% from 0.5B to 72B and −20.94% in reverse when transferring the published exponent across training setups.

relation.reason: The paper empirically evaluates a power-law predictor and compares its errors with an alternative; it does more than cite or assume scaling laws. The transferred-exponent comparison nevertheless leaves strict V2 untested.

tranche.reason: Section 4.4 reports its own power-law prediction errors and explicitly argues that conventional power-law prediction is less robust. This qualifies as a critical result or argument, although the comparison does not test V2's specified fitting protocol.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v7, dated 10 March 2026. The authors' conclusions are accurately summarized, but superiority over the comparator does not establish superiority over a power law refitted to the target setup.

statements.problem: The Qwen2.5 numbers and protocol description are correct; the limits_scope label is unsupported for V2 because its fitting protocol was not tested.
